text:
Drilling Operations will begin on the Ross Ice Shelf in early November, 1976. Drilling efforts will be as follows:
Water well to a depth of about 100-m.
2. Cored hole to penetrate through the ice shelf.
3. Gas extraction hole (large diameter open hole).
4. Access hole to penetrate through the ice shelf (large diameter, 30-cm, open hole).
The water well will provide a source of water for the camp as well as for drilling purposes. This well will be maintained throughout the season and the heat source will be a hot water circulating system. A submersible pump will be used to lift the meltwater to the surface.
The core hole, about 16.5 cm in diameter, will be cased in the upper 75-m or to a well below the firn*-ice interface. After drilling to a depth of about 300-m using air as a drilling fluid, a liquid, probably DFA (Diesel Fuel Arctic) will be introduced into the hole to reduce closure by creep to an acceptable level by establishing a hydrostatic pressure slightly less than that in the ice. When this hole bottoms out seawater will rise up into the hole and freeze rather quickly. This will prevent the loss of any drilling fluid into the sea water below the hole.

Firn is defined as compacted snow with density between 
\underline{ca.0.5}
 and 
0.8 \text{ gm/cm}^3
. Densities greater than 0.8  imply the elimination of pore spaces, are normally classified as ice, and can be considered impermeable.
